newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU grain panel meets but without export ritual.
newsitem.headline: EU grain panel meets but without export ritual.

text.p: European grain officials were meeting in Brussels on Thursday but without any of the export or import tenders to hand which make their closed-door meetings a weekly obsession for grain markets.

Cereals management committee members discussed rice and standing processed product refunds at expert-level talks on Thursday morning and were due to tackle the same subjects, including a routine rice export tender, in the afternoon.
But market-driving grain export tenders are closed and a 550,000 tonne quota for preferential maize to Spain was used up at the last session, leaving the formal agenda almost blank.
It was not finally clear whether the Commission intended to put forward new grain export tenders for the coming 1997/98 (July/June) season at Thursday's meeting.

But chances were seen as mixed since the issue was not among the topics for dicussion circulated before the meeting and EU agriculture director Guy Legras had stated firmly on Tuesday that Brussels was "not in a hurry" to open the tenders.
The Commission can make a proposal to open the tenders, at which traders bid for subsidies, without putting it on the agenda. But it does not usually do so without prior warning.
The EU began blocking exports in April, towards the end of a 1996/97 (July/June) season that saw a 57 percent increase in total cereal export volumes.
The Brussels-based Commission is concerned about forcing up domestic grain prices, contrary to the aims of a 1992 farm reform, if exports are allowed to flow freely.
Legras said more would need to be known about the summer grain harvest before taking a decision to open the tenders.
Doing so does not immediately signal exports since the Commission remains free to reject bids for subsidies, and traders say demand would in any case be thin for a while.
But such a move would be seen as a message that the Commission was prepared to renew its broken contact with the world market and could prop up domestic prices, traders said.
The EU panel was due to set standing refunds for processed products, as it does at the last session each month.
